consensus_summary: Wall primarily symbolizes divine protection, security, and salvation (God as wall of fire; walls called Salvation), with broken walls as vulnerability/judgment; common alternatives include dividing wall of hostility, obstacles (Jericho), false security/whitewashed walls, and personal self-control/boundaries.
book_summary: Wall is Salvation—the covenant's enclosure (God Himself a wall of fire round about); the counterfeit is self-built (wealth as high wall in conceit; whitewashed wall of false peace that the storm flattens).
book_core_identification: Salvation as the covenant's enclosure (with God as wall of fire)
boundary_disagreement: Book narrows precision to 'covenant's enclosure' and integrally pairs the positive sense with self-built counterfeits; consensus admits broader polyvalent applications (e.g., Ephesians dividing wall, Jericho obstacle, holiness boundary) without requiring those as core.
rationale: Cores reduce to the same referent: wall as divine salvation/protection, grounded in identical key texts (Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5). Book preserves that category while refining precision ('covenant's enclosure') and extension (elevating counterfeit self-built walls of Prov 18:11/Ezek 13 as integral rather than mere alternative). No replacement of the central identification; other consensus alternatives are simply outside the book's focused cases.
strongest_objection: Consensus stresses polyvalence and the high prominence of the Ephesians 2 'dividing wall of hostility' (and Jericho) as major uses that the book's salvation/counterfeit focus omits, risking incompleteness for NT theology.
